HELOC payments in four charts: interest paid, debt remaining and a rate change

Compare paying interest alone with adding fixed principal repayments, then trace how a different rate changes the monthly cash commitment and cumulative interest.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore interest-only payments, principal repayment and a rate change

Interactive planning lab

Interest paid: interest-only / repayment52,800 / 36,768 CAD

Hypothetical HELOC balance, not an offer or lender statement. Interest is opening monthly debt × nominal annual rate ÷ 12, paid at month-end. The second path also pays fixed principal, capped at the debt remaining. The new rate starts in the month after the selected completed months. No new draws, fees, daily accrual, tax or lender minimum-payment rules. Totals cover only the selected horizon; remaining debt is still owed.

The central idea

Paying the interest can keep a balance from growing while leaving the original debt intact. Track the cash payment, principal remaining and interest cost separately.

01

Separate the payment from the progress

A debt statement contains several different planning questions. How much cash leaves the household this month? How much of that cash reduces what is owed? How much interest has been paid to use the borrowed money? A small required payment does not answer all three.

The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s HELOC guide describes a revolving credit product secured by the home. Depending on the agreement, regular payments may cover interest alone or include principal. The agency also explains that interest-only payments do not repay the borrowing.

The charts start after a hypothetical CAD 60,000 has already been borrowed. They compare two repayment habits on that same debt. This is not a recommendation to borrow, a comparison with investing the borrowed funds, or a calculation of available home equity. There is no new spending financed from the line during the illustration.

02

Read the first month in dollars

The initial nominal annual rate is an assumed 7%. Under the monthly simplification used here, first-month interest is CAD 60,000 × 7% ÷ 12 = CAD 350. The interest-only case pays that CAD 350 and still owes CAD 60,000.

The second case pays the same CAD 350 interest plus CAD 300 of principal, for a CAD 650 cash payment. Debt falls to CAD 59,700. Next month, interest is calculated on that smaller opening debt. The extra CAD 300 is a reduction of a liability, rather than another interest expense.

This distinction explains why the payment bars and cost curves tell different stories. The principal-repayment case uses more household cash now but pays less interest as its balance falls. The comparison does not invest the cash retained by the interest-only case or calculate a complete net-worth advantage. That would require another account and its own return, cost and risk assumptions.

03

A lower balance can still have a higher interest bill

The selected rate changes after twelve completed months, so month thirteen uses the assumed 9% rate. In the interest-only case, debt remains CAD 60,000 and the monthly interest payment rises from CAD 350 to CAD 450.

After twelve CAD 300 principal repayments, the other case opens month thirteen owing CAD 56,400. Its interest is CAD 423, and its total payment is CAD 723 after adding the CAD 300 principal amount. Interest has risen from the opening month despite the reduction in debt.

The FCAC describes most HELOC rates as variable and notes that changing rates can increase payment requirements. The two rates and the change date here are invented stresses. They are neither a lender quote nor a prediction about prime rates. Use an actual agreement to confirm how its rate, daily accrual, minimum payment and notice provisions work.

04

Reconcile the ten-year totals and the unpaid endpoint

Over the selected ten years, the interest-only case pays CAD 52,800 of interest and finishes with the original CAD 60,000 still outstanding. The total is CAD 4,200 for the first year plus CAD 48,600 for the next nine years at the higher assumed rate.

The principal-repayment case pays CAD 36,000 toward principal and CAD 36,768 in interest. Its total cash payments are CAD 72,768, and its ending debt is CAD 24,000. The liability check is CAD 60,000 − CAD 36,000 = CAD 24,000. The cash-payment check is principal repaid plus interest.

The modeled interest difference is CAD 16,032 within this window. It is not a lifetime interest saving: neither default path has fully repaid the line by the endpoint. Future rates, later repayments and new draws could change the eventual total. Extend the horizon or increase principal payments to see when the second balance reaches zero; the tool then stops collecting payments.

05

Use the matrix to test a repayment habit

The matrix replaces the later rate and the monthly principal repayment. Each cell totals interest over the selected horizon while retaining the opening balance, first rate and change timing. Read across one row to isolate principal repayment; read down a column to isolate the later rate.

Because principal is a fixed amount above interest, its repayment schedule does not slow automatically when rates rise. Instead, the required cash payment rises. A real household with a fixed total payment budget would need a different model: more interest would leave less room for principal. Do not confuse these two payment rules.

No redraw is assumed. If CAD 300 is repaid and then borrowed again to cover another expense, debt will not follow the declining line shown here. An effective review therefore checks both the repayment transfer and subsequent use of the facility.

06

Connect the schedule to the household budget

Start with a supported opening balance and the actual rate formula. Choose a principal amount that fits the budget alongside required housing payments, other debt and a cash reserve. Then test a higher interest rate without silently reducing that principal target.

List any setup, administration, legal or discharge charges separately; the charts exclude them. Interest is modeled as a nominal annual rate divided by twelve on the opening monthly balance, rather than an actual daily lender ledger. No interest deduction or other tax benefit is assumed.

The home secures a HELOC, so a manageable-looking monthly payment should not be read as proof that the borrowing is suitable. The practical output of these charts is a set of explicit commitments: the monthly cash needed under a rate stress, the intended pace of principal reduction, and the date at which the remaining liability must be reconsidered.
